results.caption: my family of 5 lived off $28,000 a year in NYC, and as the eldest daughter of mexican immigrants, i watched my parents sacrifice so much to give us opportunities they never had 🥹 i almost didn't go to college. i graduated with debt. i worked multiple jobs. i got rejected over and over again. and i cried A LOT along the way. but i also met incredible people who believed in me, opened doors for me, and helped me get to where i am today. at 30, i've accomplished things little viv could've never imagined... tbh i still can't believe this is my life ❤️ i share my story not because i believe hard work alone can overcome poverty because that's not true. systemic barriers are real, and so is privilege!! but i do hope it inspires you to keep going, even when life feels really fu*king unfair thank you for being part of my journey. over 200,000 of us breaking cycles and building wealth together 🇲🇽 now it's your turn... what's your story? 🫂👇🏽 #overcominggenerationalpoverty #mexicanrichgirlseries #escapingpoverty #personalfinanceforlatinas #moneyforlatinas

media.transcript: Life really is unfair, but I hope my story inspires you to keep going. I'm Viviana, and this is the story of how I overcame generational poverty and became a self-made Mexican rich girl. And I'm sorry ahead of time for getting emotional, but sometimes I just can't believe that this is my life. My parents are immigrants from Mexico. They both have citizenship now, but my mom was undocumented during my childhood. My dad has always worked at a garage parking cars, and now he's a porter. My mom used to clean houses, babysit kids, and then when my sibling was diagnosed with cancer, she took care of them full-time. We grew up off $28,000 a year, family of five, and I was the eldest daughter. So I had to do a lot of translating, helping with my younger siblings, and overall just carrying a lot on my shoulders. My parents came to the U.S. to escape poverty and violence, so they always told me, Estudia, mija, estudia. So I did. And thankfully, I went to good public schools in Manhattan, so I was exposed to a lot of middle class and upper middle class kids. But I remember crying often because I wanted things that we couldn't afford, like books from this classic news fair. And every time I cried, my mom would always tell me, No te preocupes, mija, cuando estés grande, te vas a comprar eso y más. But I didn't understand back then. I was so angry because I missed out on so many opportunities because we didn't have money for them. I missed out on prom, SAT tutoring, and extracurriculars for college. But me being hard-headed, if I really wanted it, I would figure it out. When it came time to apply to college, I filled out the FAFSA all by myself. I did everything on my own. My parents didn't understand, and on top of that, I didn't want to bother them because they were dealing with a lot. We got an eviction notice. My sibling was still battling cancer and we were just overall struggling. So when I got into a few private schools, I was so happy, so proud, but I didn't know how expensive college was. So when the financial aid came in, even after scholarships and loans, we couldn't afford it. So I cried and I remember thinking, why is life so unfair? I worked so hard to get here. For what? And so there I am watching everyone on Facebook post what college they were going to, parents dropping them off. And I was like, you know what? I'm not going to give up. So the summer before college, I had done a free program at CCNY, which is a community school. And community schools are super cheap. They're public city schools. So I emailed the dean from that summer program and I asked him if he could help me since I would be applying super late. And honestly, I owe him so much because he did respond. And I was probably able to go to college because of him. I applied late to three community schools and I got into all three. And my financial aid covered all of it. So I commuted and I studied computer science at CCNY for a year before I discovered that I was pretty good at finance and economics. So I transferred to Baruch College and I met my boyfriend, now husband. I also worked while I was in school because I had to support myself and also help my family. Right before graduating, I went to the law school counselor at Baruch. She basically laughed in my face when I told her that I wanted to go to law school and become an immigration attorney. She said, with what money? So I graduated in 2018 and I became a teacher through the teaching fellows program. I became the first person in my family to ever have a salary job. My salary was $57,000 and I thought that I was rich because my dad had only ever made $28,000. But I still had a lot of debt, I was helping my parents, and I was paying for grad school out of pocket. And because I had volunteered with the mayor's office of immigrant affairs in college, I had a connection with a school in Jamaica, Queens. So I taught there for two years. In my second year of teaching, I was able to get a second job at the Legal Aid Society for $50,000. Which, if you don't know it, it's a big non-profit. And I thought, okay, this experience is definitely going to help me get into law school. So I was working two jobs, living at home, paying off my debt, and I realized that the legal space just wasn't for me. So I tried to pivot into tech and I was rejected for months. So finally, this woman gave me a chance. The youngest black woman to ever own her own fintech banking app. She gave me a contract roll for $57,000, but I had to move to Atlanta. At this point, I'm fully debt free from working the two jobs. And I started getting serious about educating myself on investing and financial literacy. I started this page to document everything and I kind of treated it as my personal diary. So I moved to Atlanta with my boyfriend, now husband, because he also quit his job to do a coding bootcamp. And mind you guys, we knew no one in Atlanta. took a huge risk and i cried so much because i didn't want to leave my family behind but i did it anyway and through this page i met astrid and nicole they were the first latina woman in my life that had ever talked openly about money to me they told me how much they were making they encouraged me to advocate for myself to ask for more to apply to other jobs because they themselves were making six figures and so it was the first time in my life that i had ever seen somebody like me achieve something that felt so impossible and at this contract job in atlanta i was hustling working seven days a week nights so i was getting super burnt out and my boyfriend now husband wasn't having any luck finding a job after graduating from his boot camp so i quit my job and we decided to move back home luckily that same week that we moved back we both got offers and we both negotiated for the first time in our careers i landed my first six-figure job once i got that job i worked my ass off to get promoted but after two years i was passed over at this point in my life i had savings and i was finally able to max out my roth ira i was still helping family financially and on And on top of that, my fiance, now husband, and I were saving for our wedding. We were living in an $1,800 rent-stabilized apartment in Astoria. Technically, we could have afforded a nicer apartment, but we were just focused on saving and investing as much as we could. I wanted to move out of the apartment, but I didn't want to pay crazy New York City rent, so I applied to the New York City housing lottery every single day. And I ended up getting one in Brooklyn for $2,200. And then after two years of being at my job, I finally decided to look for another one, and thanks to my network, I landed a $150,000 job. Around that time, my fiance was also being recruited and he ended up getting a new job for $130,000. So this is where everything really changed because we were able to then max out our 401ks and our Roth IRAs and give back to our families and save for our wedding. We had a four-year-long engagement, but we were able to have our dream wedding in Mexico and pay for some family's travel and their stay while still saving and investing aggressively. All of that I've documented on my page. From paying off my debt to investing my first $100,000, getting married in Mexico to eventually leaving my six-figure job to pursue this little business. and now here we are october 16th 2026 i'm happier than i've ever been i'm richer than i ever thought i would ever be and i still cry today because i can't believe that this is my life i cry because my mom was right but the best part about my life is that now i help other people do the same because i know that i'm one of many many mexican girls that overcame the cycle and now there are 200 000 of you now it's your turn i want to know it's your story if you feel comfortable sharing i would love love love to read it in the comments

school out of pocket. And because I had volunteered with the mayor's office of immigrant affairs in
college, I had a connection with a school in Jamaica, Queens. So I taught there for two years.
In my second year of teaching, I was able to get a second job at the Legal Aid Society for $50,000,
which if you don't know it, it's a big non-profit.
And I thought, okay, this experience is definitely going to help me get into law school.
So I was working two jobs, living at home, paying off my debt.
And I realized that the legal space just wasn't for me.
So I tried to pivot into tech and I was rejected for months.
So finally, this woman gave me a chance.
The youngest black woman to ever own her own fintech banking app.
She gave me a contract role for $57,000, but I had to move to Atlanta.
At this point, I'm fully debt free from working the two jobs.
And I started getting serious about educating myself on investing and financial literacy.
I started this page to document everything and I kind of treated it as my personal diary.
So I moved to Atlanta with my boyfriend, now husband, because he also quit his job to do a coding boot camp.
And mind you guys, we knew no one in Atlanta.
Took a huge risk and I cried so much because I didn't want to leave my family behind.
But I did it anyway and through this page, I met Astrid and Nicole.
They were the first Latina woman in my life that had ever talked openly about money to me.
They told me how much they were making.
They encouraged me to advocate for myself, to ask for more, to apply to other jobs, because they themselves were making six figures.
And so it was the first time in my life that I had ever seen somebody like me achieve something that felt so impossible.
And at this contract job in Atlanta, I was hustling, working seven days a week, nights.
So I was getting super burnt out.
And my boyfriend, now husband, wasn't having any luck finding a job after graduating from his boot camp.
So I quit my job and we decided to move back home.
Luckily, that same week that we moved back, we both got offers.
And we both negotiated for the first time in our careers.
I landed my first six-figure job.
Once I got that job, I worked my ass off to get promoted.
But after two years, I was passed over.
At this point in my life, I had savings and I was finally able to max out my Roth IRA. I was still
helping family financially. And on top of that, my fiance, now husband, and I were saving for our
wedding. We were living in an $1,800 rent-stabilized apartment in Astoria. Technically, we could have
afforded a nicer apartment, but we were just focused on saving and investing as much as we could.
I wanted to move out of the apartment, but I didn't want to pay crazy New York City rent. So
I applied to the New York City housing lottery every single day. And I ended up getting one in
brooklyn $2,200 and then after two years of being at my job i finally decided to look for another one
and thanks to my network i landed a $150,000 job around that time my fiance was also being recruited
and he ended up getting a new job for $130,000 so this is where everything really changed because
we were able to then max out our 401ks and our Roth IRAs and give back to our families and save
for our wedding we had a four-year-long engagement but we were able to have our dream wedding in
mexico and pay for some families travel and their stay while still saving and investing aggressively
All of that I've documented on my page.
From paying off my debt, to investing my first $100,000, to getting married in Mexico, to
eventually leaving my six-figure job to pursue this little business.
And now here we are, October 16th, 2026.
I'm happier than I've ever been.
I'm richer than I ever thought I would ever be.
And I still cry today because I can't believe that this is my life.
I cry because my mom was right.
But the best part about my life is that now I help other people do the same because I
know that i'm one of many many mexican girls that overcame this cycle and now there are 200 000 of

Równo rok od zakończenia Wystawy Światowej Expo 2025 Osaka, Kansai. To okazja do wspomnień i refleksji o działaniach zrealizowanych podczas Expo i w ślad za nim, o zbudowanych przez PAIH relacjach partnerskich i relacjach nawiązanych przez partnerów PAIH i wzmacnianych każdego dnia po zakończeniu Wystawy. To czas na dumę, poczucie satysfakcji i przekonanie, że świadomość, iż budowanie MARKI POLSKA na świecie jest zadaniem nas wszystkich i tylko współpraca międzysektorowa, duma, kreatywność i odwaga zagwarantować mogą sukces równy sukcesowi Polski na Expo 2025! Dziękujemy wszystkim partnerom projektu - instytucjom, regionom, firmom, uczelniom, artystom, fundacjom, studentom. Dziękujemy wszystkim, którzy w zespole Expo w PAIH pracowali na ten sukces.

Exactly one year has passed since the closing of Expo 2025 Osaka, Kansai, Japan. This is an opportunity to look back and reflect on the initiatives carried out during and after Expo, on the partnerships built by PAIH, and on the relationships established by PAIH’s partners and strengthened every day since the Exhibition ended.

It is a time for pride, satisfaction and a firm belief that building the POLAND BRAND worldwide is a shared responsibility—and that only cross-sector collaboration, pride, creativity and courage can ensure success on a par with Poland’s achievements at Expo 2025!

We thank all our project partners—institutions, regions, companies, universities, artists, foundations and students. We thank everyone who worked as part of PAIH’s Expo team to make this success possible.

2025年大阪・関西万博の閉幕から、ちょうど1年が経ちました。万博の会期中、そして閉幕後に実施されたさまざまな取り組み、ポーランド投資・貿易庁（PAIH）が築いたパートナーシップ、さらにPAIHのパートナーの皆様が築き、閉幕後も日々深めているつながりを振り返り、その意義を改めて考える機会です。

今こそ、誇りと達成感を分かち合い、世界における「ポーランド・ブランド」の構築は私たち全員が担うべき使命であること、そして、分野を超えた協力、誇り、創造性、勇気こそが、2025年大阪・関西万博でポーランドが収めた成功に並ぶ成果をもたらすのだという確信を新たにする時です。

本プロジェクトにご協力くださったすべてのパートナーの皆様―各機関、地域、企業、大学、アーティスト、財団、学生の皆様に、心より感謝申し上げます。そして、PAIHの万博チームの一員として、この成功のために尽力したすべての皆様に感謝いたします。

一ヨーロッパにおける農林水産・食品産業の中心地
ポーランドは今、ヨーロッパを代表する食品輸出国として、その存在感を一層高めています。
2024年、農業・食品の輸出額は過去最高の535億ユ一口を記録。
高品質で安全な食料供給国として、国際市場からの信頼を獲得しています。
EU最大のリンゴの生産国であるほか、
ポーランド産の牛肉はその安全性と味わいの良さから、
日本国内でも高い評価を受けています。
近年、ポーランドによる対日食品輸出額は急増しており、過去5年間で30％の成長を達成。
これは、ポーランドの食品産業が、最新の生産技術と厳格な品質管理のもと、
安心と美味しさを両立していることの証しです。
ポーランドはさらに、精密農業や自動化技術の導入、革新的なコールドチエーン物流の構築
にも力を入れ、農場から食卓まで一貫した品質を守り続けています。

results.caption:
Here's how VCs find companies to invest in.

#venturecapital #tech #vc #startups #invest

media.transcript: Let's chat about where venture capitalists find companies to invest in. For starters, just keep in mind, where is that VC focus for their fund strategy? So there's the concept of seed investors or there's multi-stage investors, which means they invest in pre-seed, seed all the way up through IPO. In our case, we are seed investors. So we are looking for companies and the strategy is different that are just getting formed. We want to be the first institutional capital that founders have taken. It is so busy right now that I'd say my answer would be different from a year ago and that there are so many people starting companies there are so many talented smart researchers leaving lab starting companies that we are trying to get a little bit more focused and what by that i mean normally there's like this catch-all of like we get a ton of inbound through our social channels because we're everywhere we are friends with everyone we're hosting dinners everywhere and so everybody's always like pinging us like either like we get a lot of cold inbound or warm just through like a lot of the events and stuff that we do the highest quality access that we get is through our founders and operators so they have friends leaving companies that's like the alpha the only alpha left where they'll like recommend us and say like we've had such a great experience with the call on our cap table like you have to meet her the and so i'd say like that is like the best quality that we get however it has to be on thesis so a lot of times we get warm intros but they're building in categories like crypto or something that we don't invest in so like my favorite are like founder operator led intros which is like just great referrals other vcs will send us deals they're looking at it might be too early for them like they just don't feel comfortable yet or they want to see things proven out but they know that we have an appetite for that so that's another the cold stuff is hard because i get hundreds per day so it's hard to filter through everyone reaching out if we don't have a warm connection at all or don't have any mutuals that is usually not a priority for me because it's too much work and a lot of risk there is a lot of fraud in this industry weird people doing weird stuff and so i tend to shy away from like true cold cold inbound so please find a warm intro it's usually the best opportunity And then there's a lot of accelerators. So there's Speedrun, Andreessen Speedrun. There's Neo's residency program. There's YC. A lot of VCs flock to that because honestly, I kind of think it's lazy. They've done all the hard work. The deals are more expensive, but they've vetted the founders. They've made sure they're legitimate. So they're kind of in the network. And then you can cull through some of the, I guess, better quality founders that are building companies. Again, every VC flocks to that though, the multi-stages and the smaller funds that I just think it's a bit noisy and saturated. So there are amazing companies that come out of this. YC is insane, you know, performance. So does Neo. Speedrun's really impressive. We've done a few deals from there. I'm actually really impressed with speedrun. So we do spend a lot of time paying attention to that. And then if there's big conferences, like Money 2020 is still great for fintech and then re-industrialized in Detroit, it's actually really high quality. So we're always trying to figure out like what are the best events per year that we should be going to. So I would say get really close to other builders that have raised VC, get warm intros, try to get in a network. But like hitting me up cold from like somewhere in Alabama, it just isn't ever going to be a priority. And so, yeah, I hope that helps.

media.transcript: Recruiters ignore most cold messages, so here's how to make sure yours is the one that they actually open. This is day 7 on how to fix your job search so that you can get hired before 2027. Most people think that you need connections to get noticed, when the truth is you don't. You just need to give recruiters a real reason to stop scrolling past your message. So if there's a specific role you're going for and you want to get in front of the recruiter that's hiring for it, here's exactly what you need to do. Head to reslink.io and create a new reslink. Give it a unique title for the role you want and then make sure to upload your CV. Then you need to record a 60 second video pitch and you can use ResLink's Pitch AI feature to help you write it and it will give you a teleprompter so that you don't even need to memorize a thing. Now find a few recruiters on LinkedIn who are hiring for the role you want to apply to and send each one a short, personalized message with your ResLink link. One link with your CV, LinkedIn and a video pitch all in one place. So instead of being another name in their inbox, they get to see and hear you before you've even spoken to them in the first interview. And this is how you make sure that recruiters never ignore you again. So comment ResLink and I'll send you the link and don't forget to follow us for day 8.

media.transcript: The startup I was working at raised $40 million and I decided to quit my job the same day. Today I want to tell you why and what I'm doing next. If you're new here, hi I'm Hannah. I'm a former banker and Wharton MBA who pivoted to tech and marketing. Two years ago I started this account to build my non-linear career and creator business in public. I went from getting maybe a thousand views on my first video ever to growing a following of 100k, 300k because a lot of you resonated with this idea of being highly ambitious but on an unconventional career path and redefining success on your own terms. Because of my personal brand and posting on LinkedIn, I got a job offer to be the first marketer at a fintech startup. I got to build the marketing function from scratch, launch so many products I lost count, work with an amazing team, and it really felt like a dream role. All the while, I was building my own business on the nights and weekends as a five to nine builder, which I talk a lot about in my content. The week we announced our fundraise was the week of Cannes, a festival for marketers and creators. Obviously, I stayed in New York that week, but I'd realized that I reached a tipping point where I had to choose between my job and my business. I am not sharing this brag, I am sharing this to show you what happens when you spend two years building career leverage. The same week my company was featured in the news for our fundraise, I was in a Bloomberg article. We went to the New York Stock Exchange to film a video for a company where I had already been invited twice that year because of my own name. I landed my first six-figure partnership deal and had book publishers reaching out to me about my work. And I finally realized that I didn't have to rely on an institution for prestige, income, or access anymore. So you might be thinking, then why did it still take you so long to quit? Well, I actually wrote this down. I have been conditioned as a high achiever to borrow prestige from institutions. I've always believed that the best way to learn and earn is to work for a big company, even after I gained the skills and reps I needed. So now you're probably thinking, hurry up and tell us what's next. Before I get to that, I just want to say a huge thank you. Reading your DMs and comments, seeing how you build your own five to nine businesses, and meeting so many of you virtually and in real life is what gave me the courage to actually practice what I preach. This video is getting long and I have a lot more to say about why I quit my job because it was off-brand, why corporate isn't the enemy, what I did financially before I left, and how to build options like this for yourself because that's what a non-linear career is all about. Stick around and I will share the rest soon.

media.transcript: This Lebanese entrepreneur went from winning international taekwondo medals to leading a fintech business in Lebanon and the region. Meet Noel Mukiver, CEO of Monty Finance, founder of Taekwondo Fighters Academy, and entrepreneur behind NFL Diet Center. His journey started long before fintech. In 2004, Noel founded Taekwondo Fighters Academy in Lebanon, turning his passion for martial arts into a business. And he wasn't just coaching, he was a competitive athlete winning a bronze medal in Asia in 2004, a gold medal the Mediterranean Championship in 2005, where he earned the title of Best Player, along with many other medals throughout his career. Over time, the Academy expanded to multiple branches across Lebanon. Then came a different arena, Digital Payments. After many years of experience in technology and digital transformation, Noel joined MontyPay in 2021, helping build its operations. The platform provides merchants with payment solutions designed to make online transactions simpler and more secure within its first 18 months the team onboarded hundreds of merchants and expanded into multiple countries and the recognition followed in 2023 the platform won best newcomer at the jordan startup expo followed by the payment innovation award at e-commerce expo uk in 2024 and starting 2026 noel is leading monte finance providing a full financial ecosystem to individuals and businesses in lebanon one entrepreneur multiple sectors and a career built around turning expertise into businesses. Follow Green Currency for more.
